name: Pastel Blue
lede: Pastel Blue is a pale, greyed blue; the word pastel names the softness, but it had an older life in French as the name of a blue dye paste made from woad.

sections.title: Pastel
sections.body: Paterson defines pastel as a pale shade or tint of a color, and says that pastel colours such as pastel blue and pastel pink are ones to which grey has sometimes been added [1]. That fits this swatch, a soft grey-blue [2]. The library's older Pastel Blue is darker: a steel-blue from RAL 5024, ISCC-NBS block 186 and Maerz and Paul, which dates the name to 1789 [2]. It sits nearest [[steel-blue]], at 7.9 units [2]. Compare [[powder-blue]] and [[sky-blue]].

sections.title: The older pastel
sections.body: In early French literature, the Pigment Compendium says, *pastel* meant the best kind of woad dye paste, and the word later came to mean the plant itself [3]. That blue is the cousin of [[indigo]]. The crayon, also called a pastel, is a separate sense, named from the paste of ground pigment bound with gum or clay [1][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units that covers at least five per cent of the canvas appears in 231 of 23,781 paintings, about 1 per cent [4]. It peaks in the 1870s, at nearly three times the archive's rate, and in Impressionism, where 10 of 140 works match [4]. Sisley has 8 of his 50, and Van Gogh's 1887 [[painting:aic-27954|Terrace and Observation Deck at the Moulin de Blute-Fin]] carries it over 40 per cent of the picture [4]. As photographed: museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test.
